title: Full persuasion of pardon is not so necessary that the weak of faith are cut off
source_text: XXXIII. Hic quoque quaestio non est, Num persuasio plena & absoluta de impetrata peccatorum venia, & sua cum Deo reconciliatione, in fidelibus tam necessaria sit, ut sine ea nullo modo justi, & accepti Deo esse possint, imo pro fidelibus haberi non debeant. Nam superiori disputatione manifestum fecimus Theologos Protestantes communiter agnoscere, multos esse fideles qui nondum adepti sunt plenam illam persuasionem, quique nimium oculos in infirmitatem propriam figentes, saepe non parum formidant & dubitant, an sint divinae gratiae participes, & fidem illam habeant cui promittitur salus & remissio peccatorum: qui propterea tamen non debent numero vere fidelium excludi, nec desinunt Deum habere propitium & placatum in Christo.
pass_a_gloss: Here likewise the question is not whether a full and absolute persuasion concerning obtained pardon of sins and one’s reconciliation with God is so necessary in the faithful that without it they can in no way be just and accepted by God, nay rather ought not to be held for faithful. For in the preceding disputation we made plain that Protestant theologians commonly acknowledge that there are many faithful who have not yet attained that full persuasion, and who, fixing their eyes too much on their own infirmity, often not a little fear and doubt whether they are partakers of divine grace and have that faith to which salvation and remission of sins is promised: who nevertheless for that reason ought not to be excluded from the number of the truly faithful, nor do they cease to have God propitious and appeased in Christ.
pass_b_english: Protestants do not make absolute assurance of pardon the gate of true faith.
Weak believers who still fear may remain truly faithful and reconciled in Christ.
